slides.title: Conditional Graph Normalizing Flows for N+QED-Controlled Molecular Generation

bullets.text: Nisha Ponnambalam
Supervisor: Prof. Simran Kaur
All experiments complete. This deck is for discussion of results.
Cells shown as — are numbers still on the cluster, listed on the 'Data still needed' slide.

slides.title: Summary

bullets.text: WORKS: the autoencoder reconstructs real molecules well.
WORKS: the conditional flow learns a strongly condition-dependent density — +3.70 nats/node between QED 0.4 and 0.8, about 14x the baseline.
DOES NOT WORK: that signal does not survive decoding into controlled QED. Requesting QED 0.4 vs 0.8 at fixed molecule size changes the decoded molecules very little.
Four interventions tried, each with a pass/fail criterion fixed in code BEFORE the data existed. All four failed their criterion.
Three of the four were rejected by a cheap read-only gate before any training was spent.
CONTRIBUTION: a decomposition of where conditional control is lost in a flow-plus-autoencoder pipeline, with each candidate repair falsified at the cheapest level that could refute it.

slides.title: Pipeline, and where the signal is lost

bullets.text: SMILES → encoder → node embeddings → flow f(x,c) → latent z
Generation: sample z | c → flow inverse → embeddings → decoder → argmax → valence-constrained assembly → molecule
Conditioning enters through FiLM blocks inside the flow and through the latent prior.
The decoder is FROZEN and was trained only for reconstruction, never for control.
The final discrete step (argmax, then valence/degree-constrained assembly) is not differentiable and was never trained jointly with the flow.
Our evidence points at this last step as where the conditional signal is discarded.

slides.title: Baselines: what to compare us against
slides.kicker: Prof. Kaur's question — this is the calibration slide
slides.note: Published validity is not measured identically across papers and most use a correction step, so our corrected column is the one to compare.

slides.title: None of those papers reports conditional QED control
slides.kicker: The closest published numbers are for property control, not validity
slides.note: Even papers that target property control report per-molecule correlations near 0.5, and one reports per-molecule rho 0.22 against a perfect group-level score. Per-molecule control is weak across the literature. That is the honest frame for our result.

slides.title: Result 1 — Autoencoder reconstruction works

bullets.text: Reading: the representation can carry the chemistry. The bottleneck found later is NOT the autoencoder's capacity on real molecules.
Caveat to state out loud: good reconstruction of REAL embeddings does not imply good decoding of GENERATED embeddings. That gap is Result 3.

slides.title: Result 2 — The flow does learn a conditional density
slides.kicker: Conditional log-likelihood gap, QED 0.4 vs 0.8, nats per node

bullets.text: Conditioning is emphatically NOT being ignored: the separation grows about 14x from baseline to final.
Whatever is wrong, it is not that the flow failed to learn the condition.

slides.source: qed_gap_decomposition.json, job 366922 — telescoping identity verified to 8.9e-15

slides.title: Result 3 — ...but decoded QED barely responds
slides.kicker: Final checkpoint geometry: the central puzzle of the thesis

bullets.text: At N=30 the model moves in almost exactly the right direction (+0.895) with more than enough magnitude (1.49x) — and decoded QED still hardly changes.

Our interpretation, suggested not proven: the discrete assembly step collapses a large volume of embedding space onto the same molecule, so a correct latent displacement can produce no change in the output graph.

slides.title: Result 4 — Decoder dependence: corrected vs raw validity
slides.kicker: Corrected leads, because that is what the teammates and the published papers report

bullets.text: Raw validity is kept beside corrected because the raw-corrected gap IS one of our findings — 'strong reliance on corrected decoding, especially at larger N'. Removing the column removes the finding.
Discussion question: keep raw here, or move it to the appendix?

slides.title: Result 4b — The same embedding decodes to different QED

bullets.text: Measured per generated embedding, not between population means: each saved record holds all three decodings of the SAME embedding.
If the same embedding gets materially different QED from different assemblers, then 'the QED of a generated embedding' is a property of the postprocessing, not of the model.

slides.title: Result 5 — High-QED molecules are present, so support is not the problem

bullets.text: The model CAN produce high-QED molecules. It cannot produce them ON REQUEST.
That separates a capacity problem from a controllability problem — the cleanest single argument that the failure is in conditioning rather than in chemistry.

slides.title: Result 6 — Four interventions, four pre-registered failures

rows: Numerically failed at ~step 5,400; traced to 4 inverse-only sites
surrogate must transfer to generated embeddings
Gate failed, QED arms correctly skipped (job 369665)

bullets.text: Every criterion was fixed in code before the data existed, so none of these is a post-hoc rationalisation.
Interventions 2 and 3 cost under 10 minutes of CPU each to reject.

slides.title: Intervention 2 — Anchored Conditional Prior gate
slides.kicker: dRDKit QED under a +1.0 shift along the real-QED direction

bullets.text: On REAL embeddings a latent shift moves QED (N=15, 23). On GENERATED embeddings it does not. No monotonic response anywhere.
Honest limitation: the N=15 real arm had only 14 samples and is underpowered. We do not lean on it.

slides.title: Intervention 3 — Why the surrogate gate mattered
slides.kicker: QED surrogate validated BEFORE any guidance was applied

bullets.text: Both feature sets failed on generated embeddings, so the QED-guidance arms were skipped by design rather than run against an unreliable critic.
The manifold-only arm (no learned critic) did run: it improved QED MAE in 2 of 9 conditions.

slides.title: The trap we avoided — why a response number alone is not success
slides.kicker: Manifold-arm guidance at N=30: native vs guided decoded QED

bullets.text: Headline 'response' rose from +0.130 to +0.255 — which looks like success.
It came entirely from pushing LOW-QED samples lower, not from reaching 0.8. A response number without the per-request breakdown would have been reported as an improvement.
This is why our success criterion requires the paired response AND preserved chemical quality, never MAE alone.

slides.title: Scale dependence — what looked good small, and what held up
slides.kicker: The slide I would most like your advice on

bullets.text: Several promising-looking numbers appeared at 8-10 samples per condition and did not survive at 100.
At n=10 the confidence interval on a QED mean is roughly +/-0.1 — the same size as the effect we are chasing. A small-sample headline would not survive the first question about n.
Discussion question: is the sample-size sensitivity itself worth a thesis section? It is a real, reusable finding about evaluating conditional generators.

slides.title: A statistical error we found and fixed in our own evaluation

bullets.text: BEFORE: 'improvement' was declared when the fine-tuned model's response interval excluded ZERO.

Why that is wrong: it asks whether the new model responds at all. It does not ask whether it responds MORE than the old model. Two models can both exclude zero and be statistically indistinguishable from each other.
AFTER: the test is on the DIFFERENCE between models, with Holm correction across the three N.

Limitation we state rather than hide: the per-molecule deltas were not saved, so the exact paired test is unavailable. We report a conservative bound — shared prior noise makes the models positively correlated, so assuming independence overstates the error.
Consequence: a non-significant result here is INCONCLUSIVE, not proof that the models are equal.

slides.title: Definitive comparison table

bullets.text: Protocol identical for every row: one prior-noise draw per N reused across all checkpoints and all QED requests; temperature 0.2; 100 samples per cell; degree-corrected decoder; response = per-molecule QED difference between highest and lowest request at fixed N, over JOINTLY VALID pairs only.

Seeds: the evaluation noise stream is distinct from the relabeling pool stream, and the code refuses to run if they coincide. Earlier stages used their own seeds, so their numbers are NOT sample-matched to this table and must not be pooled with it.

slides.title: The early-vs-final trade-off

bullets.text: Caveat we must state: the early checkpoint's responsiveness advantage is confounded with its lower validity. Low-validity models produce different molecule-size distributions, and we showed that unpaired scoring inflates QED comparisons by up to 25 percentage points.
Our paired, jointly-valid protocol is designed to remove exactly that bias.
Discussion question: report the trade-off as a finding, or control it away as a confound? We currently do the former, with the caveat attached.

slides.title: What the work establishes, suggests, and leaves open

bullets.text: ESTABLISHES
The autoencoder is not the limiting factor on real molecules.
The conditional flow learns a strongly condition-dependent density (+3.70 nats/node).
That signal does not translate into controlled decoded QED.
Four interventions fail criteria that were fixed in advance.
Decoding depends heavily on correction, increasingly at larger N.
SUGGESTS, NOT PROVEN
The loss is concentrated at the discrete assembly step: correct direction (+0.895), sufficient magnitude (1.49x), no effect on the output.
Pooled decoder statistics barely predict decoded QED on generated embeddings (correlation 0.02-0.12).
OPEN
Whether the fine-tuned model differs from the original at all — the test inputs were not saved.
Whether any gain is intrinsic or specific to the degree decoder.
Whether joint decoder training, or direct discrete graph generation, would retain the signal. We did not test this.

slides.title: Questions for you

bullets.text: 1. FRAMING. Is 'where conditional control is lost in a flow+AE pipeline, with four falsified repairs' a defensible contribution, or do you want a different frame?
2. BASELINES. Are the ZINC250K validity numbers (GraphDF Table 1) the right comparison set, or should we compare against the teammates' QM9 pipeline despite the dataset difference?
3. RAW VS CORRECTED. We lead with corrected for comparability. Keep raw as a secondary column, or move it to the appendix?
4. SCALE DEPENDENCE. Promote to a findings section, or keep as a methodological note?
5. SCOPE. We have stopped running new training interventions. Agreed?

slides.title: Appendix — definitions, so numbers are comparable

bullets.text: Raw validity — sanitisable AND a single connected component, with no repair step.
Corrected validity — after valence/degree-constrained assembly. This is what the teammates and MoFlow report; MoFlow has --correct_validity on by default.
Paired dQED at fixed N — per-molecule QED difference between the highest and lowest QED request, same prior draw, jointly valid pairs only.
Condition gap — validation NLL under permuted conditions minus under own conditions. Greater than 0 means conditioning is alive; about 0 means it is ignored.
Internal diversity — 1 minus mean pairwise Tanimoto over unique valid molecules.
nats per node — log-likelihood differences are reported per node so molecules of different size are comparable.
